papers.title: EEG-Derived Proxies of Cortical Excitability in Epilepsy: Group Discrimination, Temporal Stability and Medication Sensitivity
papers.abstract: Objective To identify EEG-derived markers of cortical excitability that best distinguish people with epilepsy from healthy controls while maintaining stability across repeated recordings, and to assess the influence of antiseizure medication (ASM) burden on these measures. Methods Scalp EEG recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Epilepsy Corpus were analyzed, including 1,404 recordings from 96 individuals with neurologist-confirmed epilepsy and 85 healthy controls across multiple sessions. Eight global EEG measures were evaluated: aperiodic exponent and offset, sample entropy, detrended fluctuation analysis exponent and derived index, spatial gamma-band phase consistency, and absolute and relative alpha power. Primary group inference used linear mixed-effects models to account for repeated recordings and sessions within participants. Secondary analyses examined group differences in measures temporal stability and cross-metric correlation. We examined only in epilepsy group associations between EEG-derived metrics and ASMs count, and their impact on cross-metric correlations. Results In the mixed-effects models, aperiodic offset and exponent were the only measures with FDR-robust group effects. Aperiodic offset showed higher consistency in epilepsy than in healthy controls (standardized epilepsy-minus-healthy beta = 0.52, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.78, FDR-adjusted p = 0.001). Across sessions, consistency was higher in epilepsy for aperiodic offset exponent (beta = 0.32, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.54, FDR-adjusted p = 0.018). Cross-metric correlation patterns were largely preserved between groups. Medication associations were examined separately within the epilepsy group. Higher ASM burden was associated with higher alpha relative power. Significance Among eight candidate EEG measures aperiodic offset and exponent differed between groups (epilepsy vs. healthy controls), and both were more reproducible across sessions in epilepsy. Relative alpha power tracked within-person antiseizure medication burden, suggesting that disease-related and treatment-related EEG markers may be complementary. These findings, obtained from routine clinical EEG in an open dataset, suggest aperiodic spectral parameters as candidates for prospective validation as biomarkers.

papers.title: Objective sleep tracking for fatigue management in cargo pilots: six months of continuous smart-ring monitoring
papers.abstract: Aviation fatigue management estimates crew sleep from rosters and self-report. We examined how sleep duration changes around flights and with departure and landing times. In an observational cohort study, 13 cargo pilots wore an Ultrahuman smart ring for six months in 2026. We linked 1,504 sleep sessions to the flown schedule. Linear mixed-effects models compared each sleep session with the same pilot's rest nights, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Total sleep time was 48 min shorter on the night before a flight (95% CI 32 to 65 min) and 28 min shorter in the first sleep after one (95% CI 13 to 43 min). Later nights did not differ. Sleep duration varied with clock time. Compared with evening departures and landings, respectively, pilots slept 57 min less before a departure between 06:00h and 11:59h (95% CI 14 to 101 min) and 97 min less after a landing between 00:00h and 05:59h (95% CI 37 to 156 min). Flight direction and length showed no association. Differences between pilots explained 14.1% of the variance in total sleep time, more than six times the 2.2% explained by duty position. Fatigue risk management could plan rest around departure and landing times.

papers.title: Impaired cortical gap-mediated inhibition in chronic tinnitus but with limited individual diagnostic accuracy
papers.abstract: Tinnitus lacks an objective marker, limiting diagnosis and treatment evaluation. We tested whether gap-mediated inhibition of cortical sound-evoked responses provides one. In a prospective, multicentre case-control study at seven sites in the United States and Europe, adults with and without chronic tinnitus heard brief pulses preceded or not by a silent gap, embedded in broadband or narrowband carriers, during electroencephalography. The primary outcome was inhibition of the N100 response. Of 584 eligible participants, 455 yielded high-quality recordings with complete covariate data (232 cases, 223 controls; mean age 45.4 years, 52% women) that entered the adjusted analyses. Inhibition was strongest for broadband noise whereas narrowband carriers gave limited dynamic range. Participants with tinnitus showed reduced broadband gap-mediated inhibition ({beta} = -19.27%, d = -0.413, cluster-corrected p = 0.002), scaling with tinnitus severity (covariate-adjusted {surd}THI model: partial R2 = 0.049, p = 0.0015). In contrast, discrimination of individuals was limited (AUC 0.612, 95% CI 0.560-0.663). Cortical gap inhibition is a reproducible group-level effect rather than an individual diagnostic test.
